chunks: "I read 'ground probe' two ways, and they're the same idea.
On the board, a ground probe point is a pad connected straight to the ground plane, with several vias, placed right next to a signal test point.
The reason is that a scope measures the difference between the tip and its ground clip, and on a fast signal that return path matters.

A long alligator lead adds around a hundred nanohenries or more, which rings with the probe capacitance and picks up noise, so a 1 nanoseconds edge looks like it has overshoot that isn't really there.
If I give the engineer a ground pad a couple of millimetres from the signal pad, they can use a spring tip or a short wire and the loop is tiny.
In a production fixture, ground probes are the pins that contact ground pads to give the tester a solid reference.
You want several, spread around the board, so each region has a nearby return.
So I'd use them whenever a signal is fast or sensitive, essentially every test point on a fast or analog net, and for power rails when measuring ripple, where I'd want a ground pad next to each.
For slow DC signals a single ground point is fine, and a good rule is about one ground pad for every one or two signal test points."
